article_title: Pre-K Mathematics
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023, September). Pre-K Mathematics. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Linked classroom and home caregiver-child math activity model for early mathematics
description: This instructional pattern pairs weekly teacher-led small-group classroom math activities with caregiver-child home activities linked to the classroom content. Each classroom activity includes "a core lesson as well as additional activities to tailor the lesson for lower- and higher-performing children" and scaffolding suggestions for common errors. Home packets contain the activity, manipulatives, and a bilingual caregiver letter with a picture strip depicting how to conduct the activity.
requirements: Teacher training in implementing the curriculum with fidelity and in progress monitoring, plus ongoing in-class coaching
constraints: Implemented in Head Start and state-funded preschool settings with low-income families; effects on non-mathematics domains were uncertain
target_learners: preschool children ages approximately 3.4 to 4.5 years from low-income families
target_learning_goals: early mathematics achievement and informal mathematical knowledge
examples: In the five reviewed studies, teachers implemented small-group sessions of 4–6 children lasting 15–20 minutes, twice a week for 24–29 weeks, and sent home caregiver-child activity packets every 1–2 weeks

article_title: Student Empathy Interviews: An Instrument For Considering More Inclusive K-12 Computing Pathways
citation: Pati Ruiz, Kelly Mills, Quinn Burke, and Merijke Coenraad. (2021). Student Empathy Interviews: An Instrument For Considering More Inclusive K-12 Computing Pathways. Digital Promise White Paper. https://bit.ly/36szXLy
title: Listening to student voices is an essential feature of inclusivity efforts in computing education
description: This principle holds that districts designing inclusive computing pathways should treat listening to student voices as an essential, prioritized feature of their inclusivity efforts, rather than relying solely on adult perceptions. The paper's third finding states that "listening to student voices within the district is an essential feature of inclusivity efforts--and a priority." It works by having educators conduct empathy interviews with students about their CS/CT experiences and using what students identify to inform pathway design, especially where adult assumptions diverge from student-identified barriers.
requirements: Educators conduct empathy interviews with students about their CS/CT experiences
Districts treat student listening as a priority within inclusivity efforts
constraints: The paper offers no comparative test of listening versus not listening; the principle rests on the authors' findings from one district's work
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly minoritized students in computing programs
target_learning_goals: Broadening participation in K-12 computational thinking and computer science pathways
examples: In Iowa City, teacher committee members across high school, middle school, and elementary levels interviewed and surveyed students about their CS/CT experiences, and the district treated the findings as input to its inclusive pathway design

title: Treat literacy skills as embedded in historical thinking demonstration rather than as separate assessment categories

constraints: Applies to rubrics of historical thinking skills, not to literacy assessment itself
target_learners: U.S. high school world history students

examples: The rubrics score sourcing and historical argumentation directly rather than including separate reading or writing dimensions

article_title: How Arizona's Dropout Crisis Affects Communities, Creates Economic Losses for the State of Arizona
citation: How Arizona's Dropout Crisis Affects Communities, Creates Economic Losses for the State of Arizona. (2014). A Project of WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Lifetime-profile economic loss model for calculating social and fiscal costs of dropouts and disconnected youth
description: The report applies an established economic framework that "operates by comparing lifetime profiles" of dropouts versus graduates and disconnected versus other youth, calculating differences in earnings, taxes, health, crime, and welfare as present values. "All money amounts are expressed in present values at age 18 or age 20 using a discount rate of 3.5%", in 2013 dollars weighted to Arizona's price level. The model had been applied nationally and in other states but, as the report notes, had not previously been applied to Arizona.
requirements: National research evidence disaggregated by sex and race, Arizona-specific earnings and expenditure data, and local data from Census PUMAs, school districts, and local government departments where available.
constraints: The dropout analysis rests on a thought-experiment where at age 18 a dropout switches to being a high school graduate following the typical low-income graduate path; the disconnected-youth analysis assumes five years of disconnected status.
target_learning_goals: Quantifying economic losses from incomplete education
Informing state and local investment policy
examples: The report applies the model to Arizona and ten localities (Miami, Avondale, Mesa, Tucson, Phoenix, Goodyear, Sahuarita, Gilbert, Tempe, and Oro Valley), adapting national estimates with local educational attainment, economic conditions, and wage rate indices.

citation: Aponte ML, Vargas Sánchez AD, Chiappe A and Martínez-Pérez S. (2026). Artificial and emotional intelligence: two key forces for teachers' professional development in an era of uncertainty. Front. Psychol. 17:1935683. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935683

description: The article warns that the deepest harm of socio-emotional AI is not technical error but a pseudo-bond: an interface that resembles a relationship yet displaces it. socio-emotional growth through human interaction
examples: Table 1 lists referral to mentoring, uptake of peer-support opportunities, reduced dependence on chatbot interaction, and teacher perceptions of human accompaniment as indicators

citation: Reed Orchinik, David Rand. (2026). A light-touch AI literacy intervention helps protect against AI political persuasion. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16432
title: Light-touch AI literacy warning about LLM persuasion and selective information
description: A brief pre-conversation warning telling users that LLMs "can be 'prompted' to persuade or manipulate" and "may present information in a biased or selective way, emphasizing one side of an issue." The general version was shown identically worded in both studies; Study 2 added a specific version disclosing which direction the model was instructed to argue. article_title: Incipit: Axiom-Grounded Scaffolding for Human-AI Literary Creation
citation: Qiang Liu and Chunyi Zhao. (2026). Literary Axioms: A Conceptual Framework for Literary Creation, Interpretation, and Evaluation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25504
title: Literary Axioms framework: configuration, realization, and reader reconstruction as an interpretive cycle
description: The framework treats a literary work as the realization of a selected configuration of provisional organizing premises (literary axioms) rather than of a theme. It distinguishes an open axiom space, a selected working configuration with relations and planned realization means, the completed work, and situated reader reconstructions. As the authors state, "A work's conceptual organization can be investigated through a selected set of premises and the relations that make them jointly significant." Composition develops consequences of selected premises while reading infers organizing commitments from their realization; neither direction is a formal inference calculus.
requirements: An application must state its unit of analysis, its reading context, and the evidence available for its claims
constraints: The framework applies where a writer or reader can articulate organizing commitments and connect them to particular textual or formal choices
Where sonic, bodily, or visual experience resists propositional description, the appropriate output may be a partial configuration with an explicit remainder, or no useful configuration at all
Literary axioms are natural-language interpretations, not premises in a formal deductive system
target_learning_goals: literary interpretation
literary creation and revision
literary evaluation
examples: A worked conceptual miniature places the premises that care can require personal sacrifice and that care obligations do not extinguish personal autonomy in tension across two alternative realizations of the same scene
key_sources: Qiang Liu and Chunyi Zhao. (2026). Literary Axioms: A Conceptual Framework for Literary Creation, Interpretation, and Evaluation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25504

citation: Nicola Fuchs-Schündeln, Dirk Krueger, Alexander Ludwig, and Irina Popova. (2020). The Long-Term Distributional and Welfare Effects of Covid-19 School Closures. NBER Working Paper 27773. http://www.nber.org/papers/w27773
title: A quantitative life-cycle model of child human capital production combining public schooling investment with parental time and money investments
description: The article builds a heterogeneous-agent partial-equilibrium life-cycle model in which "public investment through schooling is combined with parental time and resource investments in the production of child human capital at different stages." The multi-layer CES human capital production function features self-productivity (higher human capital in one period raises it in the next) and dynamic complementarity (investment pays out more the higher existing human capital). Parents choose time and monetary investments, inter-vivos transfers, and children make education choices among no high school completion, high school, and college. The model is calibrated to PSID, PSID-CDS, and NLSY79 moments and used as a "quantitative laboratory" for school-closure thought experiments.
requirements: Calibrated parameters of the human capital production function, taken from the literature or matched to U.S. household micro data moments on parental investments
constraints: The model excludes innate ability complementarities: it "does not feature innate ability, only innate human capital"
The age-16 human capital process "ignores parental inputs entirely" and children's own investments, which the authors call a crude approximation
target_learners: Children aged 4 to 14 at the time of the school-closure shock
target_learning_goals: Human capital accumulation, high school completion, college attendance, and long-run earnings
examples: School and child care closures are modeled as a temporary six-month reduction in public investment ig into child human capital production

article_title: The unique role of verbal memory, vocabulary, concentration and self-efficacy in children’s listening comprehension in upper elementary grades
citation: E. de Bree, M. Zee. (2021). The unique role of verbal memory, vocabulary, concentration and self-efficacy in children's listening comprehension in upper elementary grades. First Language. https://doi.org/10.1177/0142723720941680
title: Models of listening comprehension assigning a dominant role to vocabulary, extendable to broader student-related resources
description: The article engages with models of listening comprehension that give vocabulary a dominant role across the elementary years. The authors state the findings "relate to models of listening comprehension that state a dominant role for vocabulary, also in the upper elementary years," and that the results "imply that the models could extend to evaluating broader student-related resources, such as academic self-efficacy." The study's SEM results on 442 children support the vocabulary pathway and motivate extending such models beyond linguistic skills.
requirements: Applicable to modeling listening comprehension contributors across elementary grades, including upper elementary years
constraints: The authors note findings on general cognitive resources fit a pattern of mixed findings in previous research, motivating further research into contributors throughout the elementary years
target_learning_goals: Listening comprehension of oral texts
examples: Structural equation models of 442 children's oral text comprehension, vocabulary, verbal memory, self-efficacy and concentration

article_title: Deaf Individuals’ Bilingual Abilities: American Sign Language Proficiency, Reading Skills, and Family Characteristics
citation: Freel, B. L., Clark, M. D., Anderson, M. L., Gilbert, G. L., Musyoka, M. M., & Hauser, P. C. (2011). Deaf Individuals’ Bilingual Abilities: American Sign Language Proficiency, Reading Skills, and Family Characteristics. Psychology, 2(1), 18-23. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2011.21003
title: Linguistic Interdependence Theory applied to deaf bilingual education
description: Cummins' Linguistic Interdependence Theory holds that competence in a second language is a function of proficiency in one's first language. Applied to deaf learners, the article states that "individuals who have full comma nd of ASL as a first language are better disposed to learn English as a second language". The study uses this framework to interpret its finding that ASL proficiency and reading skill correlate positively, supporting ASL as a bridge to English print.
requirements: A well-developed first language (ASL) must be established before or alongside second-language (English) instruction
constraints: The article notes the equality of ASL is not always upheld in practice, as ASL grammar courses are often not offered and no national formal ASL curriculum exists
target_learners: deaf children and adults acquiring English literacy through ASL
target_learning_goals: English reading comprehension
first-language ASL development
examples: The study measured ASL proficiency with the ASL-SRT and English reading with the WJ III Passage Comprehension subtest in 55 deaf adults

article_title: The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization
citation: Huatong Sun. (2006). The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization. Technical Communication Quarterly, 15(4), 457-481. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15427625tcq1504_5
title: Expand the design process to users' sites: treat localization as an open-ended process linking user localization back to design
description: The article argues that localization is an open-ended process reaching beyond the design stage to use and consumption, including both developer localization and user localization. Designers should not "seek to design fully localized interfaces or products (because that is never possible)" or regard shipment as the end of design. Instead they should initiate communication channels, build support networks to enhance user localization, watch use trends emerging from users' sites, and design better instrumental affordances to respond to those trends, connecting use and design on the cultural circuit.
requirements: A deep understanding of concrete use activities in local contexts while considering cultural and structuring factors
An open-system information design with built-in instrumental affordances that invite users to localize the artifact and realize its social affordances
constraints: If the dialogic interaction between developer and user localization is problematic or does not exist, the current use success might eventually dissolve or disappear
target_learning_goals: designing IT products that support user localization and postadoption use experience
examples: The author suggests designers of mobile messaging applications examine fun communication and relationship communication practices in the two cultural contexts and ask what design features could support these two types of communication work

article_title: From scribbles to scrabble: preschool children’s developing knowledge of written language
citation: Puranik, Cynthia S., Lonigan, Christopher J. (2011). From Scribbles to Scrabble: Preschool Children's Developing Knowledge of Written Language. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9220-8
title: Linearity Hypothesis of writing development: universal features precede language-specific features in a sequential continuum
description: The Linearity Hypothesis holds that writing development proceeds in sequential steps: children first master universal features of writing (linearity, segmentation, lack of iconicity) that reflect the symbolic representational nature of writing, and only then acquire language-specific features such as directionality and symbol shapes. The article contrasts it with the Unified Hypothesis, which predicts simultaneous, unordered acquisition. The study's Guttman scaling results provide "clear evidence for sequential acquisition of writing features," supporting the Linearity Hypothesis.
requirements: Assessment across multiple writing tasks, since single-task evidence (e.g., name writing only) can appear to support the Unified Hypothesis
constraints: The article notes children as young as 3 display language-specific knowledge earlier than Tolchinsky reported, and left-to-right orientation emerged in conjunction with universal features
target_learning_goals: understanding the developmental sequence of written language features
examples: Guttman coefficients of reproducibility of .94 (Write Name) and .98-.99 (composing tasks) supported a fixed feature order
key_sources: Puranik, Cynthia S., Lonigan, Christopher J. (2011). From Scribbles to Scrabble: Preschool Children's Developing Knowledge of Written Language. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9220-8

article_title: Distractibility during retrieval of long-term memory: domain-general interference, neural networks and increased susceptibility in normal aging
citation: Wais, P. E., and Gazzaley, A. (2014). Distractibility during retrieval of long-term memory: domain-general interference, neural networks and increased susceptibility in normal aging. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00280
title: Limited cognitive control resources account for susceptibility to distraction during demanding retrieval and categorization
description: The article proposes that distraction harms memory and categorization because limited cognitive control resources must both guide selection of relevant mnemonic or perceptual details and suppress irrelevant external input. The authors state these resources "have the capability to resolve interference from distractors during tasks of moderate effort" but are overwhelmed when episodic retrieval or prototype categorization adds further demands. The fMRI and rTMS findings locate the control source in left VLPFC connectivity with hippocampus and LOC.
requirements: Tasks must place demands on top-down selection of goal-relevant mnemonic or perceptual details for the resource limitation to matter
constraints: The article states the precise locus where bottom-up distraction interferes with LTM representations remains unclear
target_learners: younger and older adults performing episodic retrieval and categorization tasks
target_learning_goals: retrieval of detailed episodic memories
discrimination of goal-relevant perceptual features during categorization learning
examples: fMRI showed the hippocampus-VLPFC-LOC network's connectivity declined with visual distractors and no longer supported episodic retrieval

article_title: Interaction of threat and verbal working memory in adolescents
citation: Patel Nilam, Vytal Katherine, Pavletic Nevia, Stoodley Catherine, Pine Daniel S., Grillon Christian, Ernst Monique. (2016). Interaction of Threat and Verbal Working Memory in Adolescents. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.12582
title: Limited cognitive resources account of the threat–working memory interaction
description: The article's central explanatory framework holds that anxiety and cognition compete for a shared pool of cognitive resources whose availability depends on task load. As the authors state, "low-load cognitive tasks leave resources available for threat to be processed and to interfere with cognitive performance, whereas high-load cognitive tasks deplete cognitive resources such that threat cannot be processed and thus does not interfere with performance." The account is used to explain both the accuracy impairment at low/medium load and the abolition of anxiety-potentiated startle at high load, in adolescents and adults alike.
requirements: A cognitive task with manipulable load levels spanning low to high resource demands
A sustained anxiety induction and a physiological anxiety measure to index threat processing
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretation of its findings, not a directly tested mechanism; neural mechanisms were not assessed and would require functional neuroimaging
target_learning_goals: maintaining working memory performance under sustained anxiety or threat
examples: In the experiment, accuracy was impaired under threat at 1-back and 2-back but not 3-back, and anxiety-potentiated startle was abolished at 3-back, matching the resource-depletion account
key_sources: Patel Nilam, Vytal Katherine, Pavletic Nevia, Stoodley Catherine, Pine Daniel S., Grillon Christian, Ernst Monique. (2016). Interaction of Threat and Verbal Working Memory in Adolescents. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.12582

article_title: Timing and Intensity of Early Intervention Service Use and Outcomes Among a Safety-Net Population of Children
citation: McManus BM, Richardson Z, Schenkman M, Murphy N, Morrato EH. (2019). Timing and Intensity of Early Intervention Service Use and Outcomes Among a Safety-Net Population of Children. JAMA Network Open. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2018.7529
title: Link pediatric primary care and early intervention records to track EI-eligible children and improve timeliness, intensity, and outcomes
description: The article proposes integrating clinical and EI program data systems as a quality-improvement framework. By linking pediatric primary care electronic health records with EI program records, systems can follow children through EI care planning and service provision and measure care quality metrics such as timeliness, service intensity, and functional outcomes together. The authors state that clinical and EI record linkages could help integrate data to track EI-eligible children and that this data system integration could serve as a framework for other institutions.
requirements: Overlapping catchment areas between health systems and EI programs so children can be linked across records
constraints: Demonstrated in one health system and one EI program serving low-income families, which the authors state limits generalizability of the results
target_learners: Infants and toddlers with developmental delays and disabilities enrolled or referred to early intervention
target_learning_goals: Timely receipt of EI care plans
Adequate EI service intensity
Improved functional outcomes in social-emotional, cognitive, and adaptive/self-care skills
examples: The study linked Denver Health and Rocky Mountain Human Services EI records using a probabilistic matching algorithm, following 722 children through EI care planning and service provision

citation: Heather Toomey Zimmerman, Susan M. Land, Lillyanna Faimon, Yu-Chen Chiu. (2023). Mobile augmented reality supporting families’ immersive collaborative learning: Learning-on-the-move for place-based geoscience sense-making. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09399-9
title: Eight linked microsites organizing a place-based MAR time-travel journey from the Ordovician period to the present day
description: A microsite is defined as "the intersection of the groups' interactions, the digital MAR content, and the physical setting." The Time Explorers app arranged eight such microsites in geologic-time order—Time Spiral Sculpture, Coral Sculpture, Limestone Boulders, Sandstone Boulders, Arched Rock Wall, In-and-Out Creek, Model Cave, and Spring Basin—each pairing a physical location with narrative MAR elements, prompts, and a photo-taking sense-making activity, plus a ninth celebratory AR-filter selfie. This lesson-level pattern lets designers connect digital content across outdoor spaces while learners move.
requirements: GPS coordinates triggering app content at each physical microsite
A guiding narrative (here, time travel) that motivates movement between sites
constraints: Designed for a children's garden in Appalachia with existing geological exhibits; content customized to that community's landform history

target_learning_goals: Placing regional landforms in geologic time and explaining rock–water interactions such as erosion and cave formation
examples: At the Model Cave, a 2-D animation showed how caves form over millions of years and families measured a stalagmite to estimate its age

article_title: Performance and acceptance when using tablets as a multiple document learning tool: do application and guidance matter?
citation: Jordan Lombard, Ivar Bråten, Cécile van de Leemput, Franck Amadieu. (2021). Performance and acceptance when using tablets as a multiple document learning tool: do application and guidance matter? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09537-6
title: LiquidText multiple document reading application on iPad Pro
description: LiquidText is a reading application for tablets that "includes several additional functions adapted to working with multiple documents". Its screen areas support navigation (overview of documents), simultaneous viewing of up to three documents with highlighting, and a workspace in which learners can "group and link extracted information to construct an integrated understanding" and write the task product. In the experiment it was used on a 12.9-inch iPad Pro with a stylus with a set of five partly conflicting documents on sun exposure and health, under guidance, access-only, and non-guidance conditions.
requirements: Students may need explicit guidance to fully exploit the application's functions
constraints: In the Access condition technical removal of functions was not possible, so participants were instructed not to use certain functions while the application code was unchanged
target_learning_goals: comprehending and integrating multiple documents
examples: Participants working in the workspace moved extracted information there, grouped consistent content spatially, and wrote their answers in a textbox within the workspace

article_title: Software scaffolds to promote regulation during scientific inquiry learning
citation: Sarah Manlove, Ard W. Lazonder & Ton de Jong. (2007). Software scaffolds to promote regulation during scientific inquiry learning. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-007-9012-y
title: Link regulative support closely to domain support so scaffolds for different purposes work in tandem
description: Because fully supported students relied on regulative support more than domain support and produced worse models, the authors argue there is "a need for scaffolds designed for different purposes to work in tandem with each other." They propose making this possible by linking regulative support more closely to domain supports and activities, and suggest future research investigate whether such integrated support yields higher use and perceived usefulness than stand-alone regulative support.
requirements: Regulative scaffolds must be connected to the domain supports and activities they should serve
constraints: In this study the PC+ hints referred students to specific helpfiles but "apparently did not go far enough in stressing that domain support would enhance their modeling work"
target_learners: secondary school science students working in dyads
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge construction through modeling
effective regulation of inquiry processes
examples: PC+ hints referred students to helpfiles, but this did not prevent PC+ dyads relying on regulative support more than domain support and producing lower-quality models

article_title: Reactivity to confidence ratings: evidence of impaired rule-learning
citation: Kit S. Double, Micah B. Goldwater, Damian P. Birney. (2025). Reactivity to confidence ratings: evidence of impaired rule-learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09413-5
title: Little and McDaniel category learning paradigm distinguishing memorization from rule learning
description: A shape categorization task in which participants learn to sort 12 stimuli into two categories ('blickets' and 'daxes') defined by a disjunctive rule about inner and outer shape form or color. Success is possible "either by learning the underlying rule or by simply memorizing the category membership of each stimulus". Ambiguous transfer items, visually similar to trained items but with rule-based membership contradicting their visual match, behaviorally distinguish the strategies. In this study, strategies were inferred solely from responses to ambiguous transfer items.
requirements: Transfer test including ambiguous items whose rule-based and similarity-based classifications oppose each other
constraints: The authors did not collect self-reported strategy use data, leaving open whether participants were aware of their strategy changes
target_learning_goals: rule-based category learning
distinguishing memorization from rule-abstraction strategies
examples: Little and McDaniel (2015) showed self-reported strategies strongly predict classification of ambiguous transfer items (r =.76)

article_title: Citizenship in the Elementary Classroom Through the Lens of Peer Relations
citation: Krijnen, M. A., Wansink, B. G. J., van den Berg, Y. H. M., van Tartwijk, J., & Mainhard, T. (2024). Citizenship in the Elementary Classroom Through the Lens of Peer Relations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09870-5
title: Lived citizenship: children enact citizenship through everyday peer behaviors and relationships in the classroom
description: The review adopts the concept of lived citizenship, in which "children are citizens already in their own ways" and enact citizenship in relation to others within their contexts. Common classroom behaviors and relationships are thus viewed as expressions of children's citizenship, making the classroom a practice ground where enacting and learning citizenship are intertwined. The review connects this to peer relations research, which views children as active agents shaped by the social classroom context.
requirements: A classroom context in which children interact and build interpersonal relationships with peers and teachers
constraints: The constructs used (prosociality, aggression, acceptance, rejection) do not exhaustively cover all citizenship competences, as the review itself notes
target_learning_goals: Social citizenship competences such as solidarity, peace, and social cohesion

article_title: One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education
citation: Tommi Kokkonen & Lennart Schalk. (2021). One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09581-7
title: Lin et al.'s taxonomy extending concreteness fading levels across mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology
description: Lin et al.'s taxonomy, presented in the article's Table 1, extends the concreteness fading sequence from mathematics to the natural sciences. The article states it is "conceptually based on the chemistry triplet," mapping the concrete level to the macro scale of phenomena observable through the senses, the faded/intermediate level to nano- or micro-scale schematic representations of atoms and molecules, and the symbolic level to chemical symbols, equations, or biochemical notation. The article uses this taxonomy to show that progressing across levels in the natural sciences varies along more than one dimension and cannot be directly aligned with mathematics progressions.
requirements: Three external representations per sequence, corresponding to the Fyfe and Nathan definition of concreteness fading
constraints: The article notes the intermediate nano/micro-scale level is less obviously aligned with intermediate examples used in mathematics, and that the taxonomy is not the only possible way to conceptualize concreteness fading across disciplines
target_learners: students in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology education
target_learning_goals: understanding concepts and principles across representational levels
examples: Table 1 maps concrete examples to the macro scale in physics, chemistry, and biology, faded examples to invisible forces, nano scale, and micro scale, and symbolic notation to symbolic or biochemical representations
key_sources: Tommi Kokkonen & Lennart Schalk. (2021). One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09581-7

article_title: Interrelations Among Achievement Goals and Achievement Emotions: A Meta-Analytic Examination
citation: Tanja Bross, Ulrike Elisabeth Nett, & Martin Daumiller. (2024). Interrelations Among Achievement Goals and Achievement Emotions: A Meta-Analytic Examination. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09931-9
title: Bidirectional goal-emotion model linking achievement goals to positive and negative emotions via perceived progress
description: The article describes a bidirectional conceptual model in which "achievement goals shape individuals' emotions, as the rate of progress made towards achieving a goal leads to the experience of certain emotions," while affective experiences (mood) in turn impact achievement goals. Built on Carver and Scheier's (1998) predictions and the 2 x 2 goal taxonomy, it generates concrete predictions: mastery-approach goals should increase positive and decrease negative emotions, performance-approach goals carry risk of anxiety and dissatisfaction, and avoidance goals relate negatively to positive emotions. The article uses this model, alongside control-value theory, as a complementary theoretical anchor for interpreting goal-emotion interrelations.
requirements: Both mastery and performance goal dimensions must be distinguished, since the model's predictions derive from these dimensions
constraints: The article notes the argument primarily focuses on the direction from goals to emotions and does not fully address the reciprocal influence of emotions on goals
target_learning_goals: understanding how achievement goals shape emotional experiences and vice versa
examples: The article derives from this model that people with mastery-approach goals should not experience negative emotions when progress is insufficient, as this signals insufficient effort without taking the self negatively into account
key_sources: Tanja Bross, Ulrike Elisabeth Nett, & Martin Daumiller. (2024). Interrelations Among Achievement Goals and Achievement Emotions: A Meta-Analytic Examination. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09931-9

citation: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2
title: The lightning-formation multimedia lesson used in Mayer and Moreno's 1998 split-attention study
description: This is the multimedia lesson on lightning formation that Moreno developed for her first major study on multimedia learning with Mayer, published in the Journal of Educational Psychology in 1998. The editorial opens the lesson with the sentence "Cool moist air moves over a warmer surface and becomes heated" and reproduces early words and graphics from it as Fig. 1. Mayer reports that "the lightning passage has been used in more than a dozen published experiments conducted at UCSB and around the world," making it a widely reused stimulus in multimedia learning research.
requirements: The lesson was designed for experiments on how people learn from words and pictures, pairing narration text with graphics as shown in the article's Fig. 1
target_learners: novice learners in multimedia learning experiments
target_learning_goals: understanding lightning formation from narrated multimedia instruction
examples: Mayer and Moreno's 1998 Journal of Educational Psychology study of a split-attention effect in multimedia learning used this lesson

description: Among the article's seven conclusions is the advice to "be a life-long learner." sustained personal development and productivity

article_title: Crosslinguistic transfer of higher order cognitive skills and their roles in writing for English-Spanish dual language learners.
citation: Kim Young-Suk Grace, Wolters Alissa, Mercado Janet, & Quinn Jamie. (2022). Crosslinguistic Transfer of Higher Order Cognitive Skills and Their Roles in Writing for English-Spanish Dual Language Learners. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000516
title: Linguistic interdependence hypothesis extended to higher order cognitive skills as underlying cross-language competence
description: The article works with the linguistic interdependence hypothesis (Cummins, 1979), which holds that L2 competence is partially "a function of the type of competence already developed in L1". It notes the hypothesis left the underlying cognitive competences "a black box" and extends the candidate set to higher order cognitive skills. Its bifactor finding — a general factor common across languages plus language-specific factors — is read as evidence that higher order cognitive skills are part of the cross-language "underlying cognitive/academic language proficiency" and likely transfer between languages.
requirements: The article states future work with an experimental design is needed to confirm cross-linguistic transfer of higher order cognitive skills
constraints: Findings are limited to Spanish-English dual language learners in primary grades in the US; the transfer interpretation is correlational, not causal
target_learners: Spanish-English dual language learners in Grades 1–2
target_learning_goals: higher order cognitive skills: inference, perspective taking, comprehension monitoring
examples: The study tested relations of English and Spanish inference, theory of mind, and comprehension monitoring tasks and their dimensionality via CFA and multiple group SEM

citation: J. Fitzgerald et al. (2014). Important Text Characteristics for Early-Grades Text Complexity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037289
title: Taxonomy of early-grades text characteristics organized by linguistic level from sounds to text density
description: Table S1 organizes quantifiable text characteristics by linguistic level: sounds in words (number of phonemes, phonemic Levenshtein distance, internal phonemic predictability), word structure (decoding demand, orthographic Levenshtein distance, syllables, sight words), word meaning (age of acquisition, abstractness, word rareness), within-sentence/syntax (sentence length, grammar link type, distance to verb, link distance), discourse (linear edit distance, word overlap, cohesion triggers, type-token ratio, phrase diversity, edit distance, Cartesian word overlap), text density (information load), and non-compressibility (compression ratio). Each characteristic has a definition, a source, a possible score range with a complexity interpretation, and multiple variable operationalizations. The taxonomy structures which characteristics were tested as predictors of text complexity.
requirements: Each characteristic must be operationalized computationally from the text (e.g., via the MRC Psycholinguistic Database, CMU Pronouncing Dictionary, or researcher computer coding)
constraints: Score ranges are specific to this study's texts, e.g., linear edit distance ran "0 (if all sentences are identical or there is only one sentence; lots of redundancy, less complex) to approximately 110 in our study"
target_learning_goals: Identifying which text features make early-reading texts more or less complex
examples: Abstractness scored 0–700 from the Paivio index; information load exemplified by comparing a highly redundant text scoring .28 with a denser text scoring .58

article_title: The Constancy of Intelligence Quotients. (A Case Study.).
citation: Lincoln, Edward A. (1922). The Constancy of Intelligence Quotients (A Case Study). The Journal of Educational Psychology, 14, 484-495. https://archive.org/details/journalofeducat14
title: Lincoln's taxonomy of causes of IQ discrepancies between successive examinations
description: The article groups the causes of large differences between successive intelligence quotients under a few general heads. These are fluctuations in ability, interest or attention; unstable or psychopathic personality indicated by failure of previously passed tests; temporary retardation of mental growth paralleling physical retardation; and deficiencies in training or environment, including unfamiliarity with English, poor health keeping a child from school, and lack of experience in superior young children. The taxonomy is built from the case analyses in the paper: "The causes of the Intelligence Quotient differences which have been pointed out in the previous case studies may be grouped under a few general heads."
requirements: Interpreting a discrepancy requires supplementary case information such as teacher reports, physical measurements and examination records
constraints: The taxonomy is derived from a small set of individual cases examined with the Stanford-Binet scale, not from a systematic experiment
target_learners: children examined at a psycho-educational clinic
target_learning_goals: accurate classification of children's intelligence for educational placement
examples: Case 49's low first IQ was traced to linguistic difficulty; case 16's rise was linked to a period of rapid physical growth

article_title: Using a willingness to wait design to assess how readers value text
citation: Amrita Bains, Carina Spaulding, Jessie Ricketts and Saloni Krishnan. (2023). Using a willingness to wait design to assess how readers value text. npj Science of Learning 8:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00160-3
title: Liking/wanting decomposition of reward as applied to reading motivation
description: The article adopts the neuroscientific reward framework in which "motivation involves at least two separable components: 'liking', or the experience of enjoyment or reward, and 'wanting', the desire to obtain a reward", and links it to situated expectancy-value theory, in which subjective task value is influenced by "task enjoyment, self-schema, later utility, and perceived costs". Unlike most reading motivation questionnaires that measure only liking, the paradigm operationalises wanting as willingness to incur a temporal cost, testing whether enjoyment indexes reward.
requirements: Measurement of both a liking component (enjoyment ratings) and a wanting component (cost-bearing decisions)
constraints: Costs used are temporal (and indirectly financial), not monetary or physical costs directly
target_learning_goals: Understanding and measuring moment-to-moment motivation to read
examples: The study offered no extrinsic motivator, so waiting reflected wanting driven by enjoyment alone

article_title: Keep it simple: streamlining book illustrations improves attention and comprehension in beginning readers
citation: Eng, C. M., Godwin, K. E., & Fisher, A. V. (2020). Keep it simple: streamlining book illustrations improves attention and comprehension in beginning readers. npj Science of Learning, 5:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00073-5
title: Limit extraneous illustrations in reading materials for beginning readers to support attention and comprehension
description: The article recommends optimizing instructional reading materials by removing illustration details unrelated to the story text while retaining relevant illustrations. It reports that "extraneous illustrations promoted attentional competition and hindered reading comprehension", and the authors state they are "not advocating for the removal of illustrations from books" but for considering children's developing attention regulation in design. The principle is grounded in the Streamlined-versus-Standard comparison and the control experiment.
requirements: Relevant illustrations that reinforce the text should be retained; only extraneous details are removed
Illustration relevance should be determined systematically, as in the adult calibration study with over 90% agreement
constraints: The comprehension assessment primarily focused on recall of key story events, assessing both understanding and memory
The effect of removing extraneous illustrations on children's engagement and motivation was not measured
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Attention to text during independent reading
examples: Half of a commercially available first-grade book (Good Job Dennis) was presented with extraneous illustrations removed after an adult calibration study classified details as relevant or extraneous
key_sources: Eng, C. M., Godwin, K. E., & Fisher, A. V. (2020). Keep it simple: streamlining book illustrations improves attention and comprehension in beginning readers. npj Science of Learning, 5:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00073-5

article_title: Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives
citation: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5
title: Distinction between light-weight and heavy-weight ontologies
description: The article distinguishes two kinds of ontology. Light-weight ontologies are vocabulary-oriented, used as metadata for semantic searches in the Semantic Web; heavy-weight ontologies are "concept-oriented. They are conceptual artifacts that intend to explicate the underlying conceptual structure of the target world" and are sometimes required to have philosophical validity. The authors concentrate on heavy-weight ontologies, arguing a heavy-weight ontology can serve as vocabulary but not the reverse. This distinction frames their entire AIED program.
requirements: Heavy-weight ontologies may need philosophical validity and grounding in a top-level ontology
constraints: The article is concerned mainly with heavy-weight ontology, which the authors state is not a matter of how ontologies are represented in computers
target_learners: AIED system developers and instructional designers
target_learning_goals: Building AIED systems on shared, theory-compliant conceptual foundations
examples: The OBO foundry biomedical ontologies compliant with the BFO top-level ontology are given as examples of heavy-weight ontology work

article_title: Instructor presence effect: Liking does not always lead to learning
citation: Wilson, K. E., Martinez, M., Mills, C., D'Mello, S., Smilek, D., & Risko, E. F. (2018). Instructor presence effect: Liking does not always lead to learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.011
title: Do not assume that learner enjoyment or perceived engagement indicates effective learning in online lecture design
description: Because learners systematically prefer and believe they learn best from formats that objectively impair comprehension, instructional designers should not rely on learner preference or enjoyment ratings as proxies for learning effectiveness. The article shows that "learners not only find online lectures with visuals of the instructor more enjoyable and interesting, they believe this format most facilitates their learning" even as comprehension suffers. Objective comprehension measures are needed alongside subjective evaluations.
requirements: Requires objective learning measures (e.g., comprehension tests) collected alongside subjective evaluations
constraints: Demonstrated specifically for instructor visuals in online lectures; may not extend to other multimedia design decisions
target_learning_goals: evaluating multimedia lecture design

citation: Lin, H. (2012). The Effectiveness of Computer-Mediated Communication on SLA: A Meta-Analysis and Research Synthesis. In L. Bradley & S. title: Meta-analytic corpus of 56 CMC studies with 282 effect sizes
description: The evidence base assembled by this meta-analysis: "The final body of meta-analysis included 56 studies" — 5 conference papers, 12 masters' theses, 12 doctoral dissertations and 27 journal articles — from which "A total of 282 effect sizes were calculated from the 56 studies which contained a combined sample of about 3,713 participants". constraints: Only one report was included per study report across several sources, and studies must have been published between 2000 and 2011.

examples: Of the included studies, 49 adopted a quasi-experimental design and only 7 adopted a true experimental design with random assignment to treatment and control groups.

article_title: Multi-level meta-analysis of whether fostering creativity during physical activity interventions increases their impact on cognitive and academic outcomes during childhood.
citation: Vasilopoulos Fotini, Jeffrey Holly, Wu Yanwen, Dumontheil Iroise. (2023). Multi-level meta-analysis of whether fostering creativity during physical activity interventions increases their impact on cognitive and academic outcomes during childhood. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-35082-y
title: Linear versus non-linear pedagogy as contrasting frameworks for teaching physical activity
description: The article contrasts two pedagogical models for physical education. Linear pedagogy involves acquiring technical skills through constant or block training with drills or fixed choreography reproduced until the motor skill is mastered, with variability limited. Non-linear pedagogy involves the teacher adjusting the task, the environment, or both: varying rules, participant numbers, using open-ended problem-solving instructions such as 'Show me any other way to...', changing space size or equipment. The article links non-linear practices to inhibiting routine movement patterns and flexibly switching between variable tasks, and notes they "can be more student-centred if applied appropriately".
requirements: Non-linear practices work especially in younger years when based on children's prior knowledge of basic movement patterns such as walking, running, jumping
constraints: The article states linear pedagogy may align with natural scaffolding of learning by executive function in the early phases until automaticity is achieved
target_learners: primary school children in physical education
target_learning_goals: motor skill learning
executive functions
creativity
self-regulation
examples: Open-ended instructions such as 'How would you do that differently?' and moving from an outdoor school field to an indoor space with different props

engagement with literature

title: Literacy and Morphemes programme
description: A Year 2 literacy intervention teaching morphemic spelling rules and sentence structure to aid spelling and reading comprehension. reading comprehension
awareness of morphemes and sentence structure

citation: Busmin Gurning & Aguslani Siregar. (2017). The Effect of Teaching Strategies and Curiosity on Students’ Achievement in Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p191
title: Three-level taxonomy of reading comprehension: literal, inferential, and critical
description: The article organizes reading comprehension achievement into three levels. Literal comprehension involves what the author is actually saying, including ideas and information explicitly stated in the text. Inferential comprehension refers to the reader's ability to establish or guess correctly the logical inference of the authors, including text-connecting and gap-filling inferences. Critical comprehension emphasizes thinking critically about text meaning and making connections between text and relevant knowledge beyond the text, and is described as the most difficult level because readers arrive at an evaluative stage.
requirements: Assessment items must address all three levels; the study's forty-item objective test covered literal, inferential, and critical comprehension
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension across literal, inferential, and critical levels
examples: The study's objective test of forty items was constructed to test reading comprehension related to literal, inferential, and critical comprehension.

article_title: Number Line Estimation with Negatives
citation: Bofferding, L., Hoffman, A., Suazo, E., & Lisy, N. (2015). Number Line Estimation with Negatives. Proceedings of the 37th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. https://www.pmena.org/
title: Linear board game with integers from -10 to 10
description: The intervention element is a linear board game labeled with the integers -10 to 10, adapted from Siegler and Ramani (2009). Players start tokens at zero, draw cards labeled 1, 2, or 3, move that many spaces, and name the numbers on the spaces they pass through, e.g., moving from -7 to -6 and saying "negative six." A special card sends all players back to -10, ensuring players traverse the full range each round; in the third session this card is replaced by cards marked -2 or -4, with players counting backwards to -10. Students played an average of 4 games in 15 minutes across three 15-minute sessions with researcher feedback on integer names and moves.
requirements: A researcher plays against each student and gives corrective feedback on integer names and counting sequences
constraints: Sessions lasted 15 minutes each, three per participant
target_learning_goals: learning negative integer names, order, and values
developing a linear representation of the integers
examples: The deck was stacked so the go-back-to--10 card appeared early, ensuring players advanced from -10 to 10 each round

article_title: The Effectiveness of Visualization, Auditory, Kinesthetic (VAK) Model toward Writing Narrative: Linguistic Intelligence Perspective
citation: Kusumawarti, E., Subiyantoro, S., & Rukayah. (2020). The Effectiveness of Visualization, Auditory, Kinesthetic (VAK) Model toward Writing Narrative: Linguistic Intelligence Perspective. International Journal of Instruction, 13(4), 677-694. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13442a
title: Linguistic intelligence as an internal factor supporting writing skills
description: Drawing on Gardner, the article treats linguistic intelligence as one of nine compound intelligences, "defined as sensitivity to spoken and written languages, the ability to learn new languages and the ability to use language to achieve goals". It comprises phonology (using language sounds), morphology (obtaining and choosing vocabulary and building morphemes and words), and syntax (managing phrases, clauses, and sentences, including compiling simple essays). The authors position it as an internal factor influencing narrative writing skills, which attending to VAK learning styles is said to accelerate.
requirements: Used in this study as the theoretical perspective framing the VAK model's effectiveness
constraints: The authors state linguistic intelligence was discussed only as a supporting theory, and due to time constraints the other eight intelligences were not explored
target_learning_goals: narrative writing skills
language skills
examples: The conclusion states that in terms of linguistic intelligence theory the VAK model is effective in improving narrative writing skills
key_sources: Kusumawarti, E., Subiyantoro, S., & Rukayah. (2020). The Effectiveness of Visualization, Auditory, Kinesthetic (VAK) Model toward Writing Narrative: Linguistic Intelligence Perspective. International Journal of Instruction, 13(4), 677-694. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13442a

article_title: Using a Linguistic Theory of Humour in Teaching English Grammar
citation: Rufaidah Kamal Abdulmajeed & Sarab Khalil Hameed. (2017). Using a Linguistic Theory of Humour in Teaching English Grammar. English Language Teaching, 10(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n2p40
title: Applying the linguistic theory of humour to grammar teaching through metaphor, pun and ambiguity
description: The article's organizing framework is the application of the linguistic theory of humour to explaining a difficult grammar topic. The researchers "worked in applying the linguistic devices of humour: metaphor, pun, and ambiguity", using these devices to explain inherent and non-inherent adjectives and to design "humorous, funny and incongruous activities which evoke laughter". The theory holds that humour arises from incongruity that learners perceive and resolve, and that resolving it focuses attention on the instructional content.
requirements: The teacher must be able to perceive and resolve humour; the article states effectiveness "depends on the students' ability to perceive and then resolve the incongruity in a humorous instruction"
Humour must be relevant to the course content and appropriate in form
constraints: The method "is very much dependent on the teacher's creativity" and "takes the most time and creativity on the part of the teacher"
Styles of humour are culture-dependent, so humour must fit the learners' culture
target_learners: EFL university students learning English grammar
target_learning_goals: Understanding inherent and non-inherent adjectives
Retention and recall of grammar rules
examples: Students were given new names as Misses inherent and Misses non-inherent adjectives and acted out sentences, while teachers acted as director of a play

article_title: The Impact of Cooperative Listening Materials Adaptation on Listening Comprehension Performance of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Mojtaba Ghassemi. (2013). The impact of Cooperative Materials Adaptation on Listening Comprehension Performance of Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n2p45
title: 20-item five-point Likert attitude questionnaire on listening, validated by expert rating and pilot reliability testing
description: The study's attitude instrument is a questionnaire in three parts: demographic information, 20 Likert-scale items (1 = strongly agree to 5 = strongly disagree) measuring attitudes toward listening, and an open-ended comment section. Items are categorized into positive-attitude and negative-attitude parts. Validity was checked by three PhD holders in TEFL rating suitability and clarity, and a pilot with 23 EFL students showed "the questionnaire was reliable (ά=0.74)".
requirements: Administration at both the beginning and end of the study to detect attitude change
Expert rating of item suitability and clarity, and pilot reliability testing
constraints: The printed scale key contains an inconsistency (both 4 and 5 labelled for disagree responses), as printed in the appendix
target_learning_goals: measuring students' attitudes toward listening comprehension learning
examples: Inter-rater Spearman correlations among the three raters ranged from .626 to .806, all above the critical value of .43 at 22 degrees of freedom

article_title: Lesson Study with Mathematical Resources: A Sustainable Model for Locally-Led Teacher Professional Learning
citation: Catherine Lewis & Rebecca Perry. (2014). Lesson Study with Mathematical Resources: A Sustainable Model for Locally-led Teacher Professional Learning. Mathematics Teacher Education and Development. https://www.merga.net.au
title: Use linear measurement representations of fractions to build understanding of equal parts, fractions as numbers, the whole, and non-unit fractions as iterated unit fractions
description: The resource kit's research-based conjectures hold that linear measurement contexts help students see fractions as amounts and support "equality of fractional parts (through iteration of the same unit); fractions as numbers (through relatively easy connection to the number line)"; attention to the whole via a stable standard measurement unit; and non-unit fractions as composed of unit fractions. Teachers' reflections confirmed the linear approach felt like an advance over area models.
requirements: Materials should let students partition a whole themselves and iterate a length unit to compose fractions
constraints: Linear measurement representation of fractions is often neglected by U.S. textbooks, so materials must be supplied externally
target_learning_goals: fraction number sense, including fraction size, equivalence, and fractions greater than one
examples: One teacher wrote she would introduce fractions using the linear model because students can more clearly see splitting a whole into equal parts than in the area model of dividing brownies

article_title: Effects of Written Corrective Feedback: A Synthesis of 10 Quasi-Experimental Studies
citation: Albatool Abalkheel & Tara Brandenburg. (2020). Effects of Written Corrective Feedback: A Synthesis of 10 Quasi-Experimental Studies. English Language Teaching, 13(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v13n7p97
title: Select a limited number of error types for written corrective feedback rather than addressing all errors in a composition
description: This principle holds that written corrective feedback should target a pre-selected, limited set of error categories rather than every error, because the meta-analysis found focused feedback positive in all cases while comprehensive feedback risked harming accuracy. The article states: "Rather than addressing all errors in a composition, the instructor should select a limited number of error types and only address those in written corrective feedback."
requirements: The instructor must determine the target error types before examining the writing, as focused feedback is defined in the article
constraints: In the reviewed studies the error type was limited to two categories (referential 'a' and 'the'); the authors note the number could potentially be increased, particularly with advanced learners
target_learners: intermediate and advanced second- or foreign-language writing students
target_learning_goals: long-term grammatical accuracy in L2 writing
examples: The focused-feedback studies in the synthesis targeted only referential 'a' and 'the', and all showed positive effect sizes
key_sources: Albatool Abalkheel & Tara Brandenburg. (2020). Effects of Written Corrective Feedback: A Synthesis of 10 Quasi-Experimental Studies. English Language Teaching, 13(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v13n7p97

article_title: Effects of Reading Strategies and the Writing Process with Written Recasts on Second Language Achievement
citation: Ramirez, H., & Jones, D. (2013). Effects of reading strategies and the writing process with written recasts on second language achievement. Administrative Issues Journal: Education, Practice, and Research, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.5929/2013.3.1.7
title: Literacy-based teaching methods pattern: reading-strategy instruction, writing-process instruction, and written recasts layered onto an established communicative curriculum
description: A lesson/unit-level design in which an established communicative second language curriculum is extended with three literacy-based components: explicit reading-strategy instruction, instruction in the five-step writing process, and written corrective recasts during drafting. The reading strategies "included the use of scanning, skimming, guessing, predicting, cognates, phonological awareness, identifying grammar structures, using a dictionary, summarizing, using graphic organizers, and connecting the reading to the participant's background knowledge." Students practiced each strategy on a small portion of an extended reading before completing it independently, and wrote key information on a graphic organizer.
requirements: One teacher trained in the literacy-based methods delivers instruction; the article arranged three training meetings plus a separate meeting on test administration and scoring
An extended reading matched to learner proficiency and tied to the initial instruction by topic, vocabulary, and grammar structures
A writing assignment of at least five paragraphs using a shared prompt, with the experimental group expected to use the writing process
constraints: The teacher could provide recast feedback on only a few sentences per student per approximately 47-minute class period
The study was limited to four classes of beginning-level Spanish students aged 12–14 whose first language was not Spanish
target_learners: beginning-level (novice proficiency) middle-school second language learners, ages 12–14
target_learning_goals: second language vocabulary and grammar achievement
reading comprehension strategy use
written production in the second language
examples: The experimental group circled cognates, underlined grammar they identified, and recorded new words with meanings guessed or looked up during the extended reading

During drafting, the teacher "provided written corrective feedback in the form of recasts", and students were encouraged to repair erroneous written output, later recognizing their own and peers' errors during revision

article_title: Building the Oral Language of Young Hispanic Children through Interactive Read Alouds and Vocabulary Games at Preschool and at Home
citation: Baker, D. L., Mogna, V., Rodriguez, S., Farmer, D., & Yovanoff, P. (2016). Building the Oral Language of Young Hispanic Children Through Interactive Read Alouds and Vocabulary Games at Preschool and at Home. Journal of International Special Needs Education, 19(2), 81-94.
title: LINK (ENLACE) intervention: interactive read alouds plus vocabulary card games for preschool and home
description: LINK is a bilingual vocabulary and language intervention adapted from dialogic reading, consisting of "a teacher professional development module to increase the quality of the read alouds in preschool, and children's breadth of vocabulary knowledge" and "parent workshops that provided parents with training on how to read interactively to their children." It uses four commercially available picture books in Spanish and English, printed picture cards labeled in both languages, and three games: the Rapid Naming Game, the Matching Game, and the Pointing Game. Teachers divide read-aloud conversations into before, during, and after reading phases with wh-questions, repetition and expansion.
requirements: One-day teacher training on interactive read alouds with practice opportunities, and 1-2 hour parent workshops conducted in Spanish every other week, with feedback visits every two weeks
constraints: The article notes it was unable to examine the differential effects of the read aloud intervention and the vocabulary games, and that the home reading frequency was based on parental self-report
target_learners: Spanish-speaking preschool English learners from low-income Head Start families
Parents and teachers of young English learners
target_learning_goals: Receptive and expressive vocabulary knowledge in Spanish and English
Children's engagement and communication skills during shared reading
examples: Teachers implemented LINK read alouds every other day for ten minutes at a time, and vocabulary games were played during small group instruction every other day
Parents received one book plus vocabulary cards at the first workshop and the remaining three books every two weeks

article_title: Engaging Pre-Service Teachers in an Exploration of the Politics of Language
citation: Cheu-jey Lee, Glenda Moss, & Elaine Coughlin. (2010). Engaging Pre-Service Teachers in an Exploration of the Politics of Language. Scholar-Practitioner Quarterly, 5(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Engaging+Pre-Service+Teachers+in+an+Exploration+of+the+Politics+of+Language
title: Linguistic activity simulating language marginalization through group language creation and forced merging
description: A classroom activity in which groups create a non-English symbolic language for the statement "I enjoy this class; it is critical," then merge successively into larger groups until one "Standard Language of the Class" is adopted and everything else is deemed non-standard. It was designed to help pre-service teachers "put themselves in the shoes of the marginalized to experience the politics of language," and was followed by written reflection at both research sites.
requirements: Groups must create languages without using meaningful English words, using symbols, pictures, or numbers instead
constraints: At Northwest University only 12 participants took part, so some worked individually or in pairs in the first round
target_learners: predominantly white pre-service teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: awareness of the politics of language
empathy with language minority students' experience of linguistic marginalization
examples: Groups used digit substitutions for letters, drew a heart for enjoy, and merged from eight groups to one class-wide standard language

article_title: Using Group Discussion with Taiwan's EFL College Students: A Comparison of Comprehension Instruction for Book Club, Literature Circles, and Instructional Conversations
citation: Shen, F.-Y. (2013). Using Group Discussion with Taiwan’s EFL College Students: A Comparison of Comprehension Instruction for Book Club, Literature Circles, and Instructional Conversations. English Language Teaching, 6(12), 58-. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n12p58
title: Literature Circles assign rotating roles within student-led discussion groups
description: Literature Circles is a discussion-centered reading approach combining teacher mini-lessons with student-led discussion. The article states that "During the discussion, group members played the assigned roles of discussion director, literary luminary, illustrator, and connector." The teacher neither provides discussion questions nor intervenes in the discussion, and interpretive authority belongs solely to students. Students are encouraged to write questions and responses in the margins of the text to use during discussion.
requirements: Assigned role structures (discussion director, literary luminary, illustrator, connector) within each discussion group.
A teacher mini-lesson of 15 to 20 minutes preceding independent reading and discussion.
target_learning_goals: interpretive comprehension of literary texts
student-led discussion of text
examples: In the study's Literature Circles lessons, students read independently after a mini-lesson, annotated the text margins, then discussed in role-assigned peer-led groups.

Using Real-time Data and Corrective Teacher-feedback as a Mechanism to Improve Children’s Reading Skills: An Exploratory Study in the Millennium Village Site of Bonsaaso, Ghana. title: Literacy Report Cards: an online interface sharing real-time assessment results with stakeholders
description: The study built an online interface displaying assessment data as "Literacy Report Cards" of the school, organized by treatment and control classes and disaggregated by grade. Data captured on Android phones via Open Data Kit was sent to formhub.org and processed into graphs at litreportcards.modilabs.org. Stakeholders including teachers, principals, MVP staff and GES could review results "within weeks of data collection", and printed copies were distributed to schools without internet access.

constraints: There was no internet access at the schools, so printed copies of the Literacy Report Cards had to be distributed to school staff
target_learners: Grade 3 and 4 primary students in rural Ghana
target_learning_goals: English literacy (letter, word, paragraph and story reading)
examples: Results were shared with schools, communities and Ghanaian Ministry of Education officials within days of data collection

article_title: Exploring the Classroom: Teaching Science in Early Childhood
citation: Dejonckheere, P.J.N., De Wit, N.L., Van de Keere, K., & Vervaet, S. (2016). Exploring the classroom: Teaching science in early childhood. European Journal of Educational Research, 5(3), 149-164. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.5.3.149
title: Light box and block task for assessing scientific reasoning in young children
description: A custom-built wooden box (23 × 23 × 6 cm) with a semi-transparent platform and internal light bulb, used with a wooden red block, serves as a low-context assessment of scientific reasoning. The experimenter demonstrates that the box lights up when the block is placed upright on one side, confounding block position and orientation, so the child must isolate variables to discover the cause. Children play freely for 75 seconds while informative and uninformative experiments are coded.
requirements: A hidden remote switch allows the experimenter to control the light; the task requires a demonstration phase and a 75-second free-play phase.
constraints: The article notes the box never lights up under the child's control, so exploratory behaviour may extinguish, though most children remain motivated within the 75-second window.
target_learning_goals: control of variables strategy
formal scientific reasoning
informative experiment design
examples: Interobserver reliability for coding the videotaped task was 0.88 (Pearson r), and pretest scores correlated with conservation scores on the Toeters math subtest (r = 0.39; p < 0.05).

title: Lighted schoolhouse: after-school programming on the school campus
description: The lighted schoolhouse model hosts events on the school campus during after-school hours to "provide a healthy, positive environment for youth." In One Life, each district assigned a staff member and events occurred biweekly, alternating between districts, including recreation, leisure, and physical activity. The authors link it to improved school bonding and home-school relations through school-community partnership and facility use beyond normal hours.
requirements: School-community partnerships and use of the school facility beyond normal school hours
A faculty or staff member assigned to assist with events
target_learning_goals: school bonding
positive school-community environment
examples: Biweekly events alternating between the two participating districts, including recreation, leisure, and physical activity

article_title: Life-Wide Learning and Early Reading Development in Twelve African and Asian Sites
citation: Dowd, A. J., Friedlander, E., Jonason, C., Leer, J., Sorensen, L. Z., D'Sa, N., Guajardo, J., Pava, C., & Pisani, L. (2016). Life-wide Learning and Early Reading Development in Twelve African and Asian Sites. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567020
title: Life-wide learning: the enabling environment for literacy spans home and community as well as school
description: The article conceptualizes the enabling environment for learning at a micro level with two components: the home literacy environment, represented by reading materials and habits at home, and the community learning environment, represented by community reading activities. A focus on life-wide learning refers to "children's engagement in enjoyable, cognitively-demanding literacy-related activities not only while in school but also throughout the rest of the day, every day." At home the enabling environment includes diverse reading materials and familial habits such as reading and talking together; outside the home it includes group or pair reading and borrowing from local mini-libraries.
requirements: Opportunities afforded through the enabling environments of both the home and the community, including diverse reading materials and supportive familial habits
constraints: Conceptualized and tested in low-resource contexts where Save the Children and World Vision work
target_learners: primary school-age children in grades 1-4 in low-resource settings
target_learning_goals: early reading skills including letter identification, reading fluency, and reading comprehension
examples: Literacy Boost operationalizes the framework through Community Action programs establishing book banks and reading camps, and reading awareness workshops for parents and community leaders

article_title: Life-Wide Learning and Early Reading Development in Twelve African and Asian Sites
citation: Dowd, A. J., Friedlander, E., Jonason, C., Leer, J., Sorensen, L. Z., D'Sa, N., Guajardo, J., Pava, C., & Pisani, L. (2016). Life-wide Learning and Early Reading Development in Twelve African and Asian Sites. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567020
title: Literacy Boost program
description: Literacy Boost is Save the Children's reading program, developed in 2008, targeting primary school-age children, their teachers, parents, and communities to develop children's reading skills both inside and outside of school, with the ultimate goal of improving children's reading comprehension. It reaches over 1.5 million children in 32 countries and consists of three main components adapted to fit the local context: in-service teacher training via monthly sessions on reading pedagogy best practices, Community Action programs establishing book banks and reading camps and running reading awareness workshops, and regular reading assessments measuring reading skills and equity dimensions.
requirements: Adaptation of the three components to fit the local context
constraints: Implemented in under-resourced home and school environments
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension, letter identification, reading fluency
examples: In 2012 a partnership with World Vision led to scale-up of Literacy Boost to 10 World Vision sites over three years
