article_title: Making Culture Happen in the English Language Classroom
citation: Yakup Doganay, Madina Ashirimbetova & Brent Davis. (2013). Making Culture Happen in the English Language Classroom. English Language Teaching, 6(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n10p11
title: Link target-culture activities to local culture through comparison
description: The article recommends that teachers connect target-culture content to students' local culture by asking them to compare situations described in the textbook with the same situations in their local environment. Teachers of experimental groups were asked to "link the situations to the local culture, asking students to compare the situations described in the textbook with the same situations in the local environment." This comparison helps students see differences between target and local cultures.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of students' local culture to design comparison tasks
constraints: The article warns that the local culture should always have a priority, for there exists a possibility of full assimilation of students into a culture different from their own
target_learning_goals: Intercultural communicative competence
Communicative competence in English
examples: Students compared friendship practices described in a textbook unit with local Kazakh, Russian, and Turkish practices

citation: Pers Michał, Kupis Robert, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Cebula Grzegorz, Szopa Magdalena. (2026). Linear virtual patients versus student role-plays in teaching patient-centeredness: a mixed-method study. International Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.6a0d.902f
title: Linear virtual patients focused on the patient's perspective implemented in the DID-ACT curriculum
description: Interactive patient scenarios presenting the patient story following the classical linear HxExIxDxRx structure, developed using the electronic case-based system and available as part of the open access clinical reasoning curriculum DID-ACT. Three hypertension cases present the same biomedical background from three perspectives (drug-reluctant patient, woman hesitating on pregnancy, man struggling with healthy lifestyle). Ideas and beliefs, and concerns were integrated into information-gathering sections, while expectations and impact on life were connected to information-giving sections (Figure 1).
requirements: Electronic case-based system to implement the interactive scenarios
constraints: Occasional technical issues encountered during sessions may have influenced outcomes
target_learning_goals: patient-centered attitudes
understanding the patient's perspective
examples: Used to replace role-plays during the patient's perspective classes in a mandatory six-meeting communication course

article_title: Construction and practice of a certification system for clinical nursing preceptors: a " license to teach" approach in China.
citation: Tang Yinying, Linyue Tan, Chen Xiuwen, Chen Huiqiong (2026). Construction and practice of a certification system for clinical nursing preceptors: a “license to teach” approach in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08953-x
title: “License to Teach” certification system for lead clinical nursing instructors
description: An institutional certification system for lead clinical nursing preceptors developed by a Chinese tertiary hospital based on its Clinical Nursing Teaching Management Standards (2021). It combines eligibility criteria (degree, experience, professional title) with a "multi-dimensional evaluation model comprising three modules: classroom teaching, skill training, and teaching ward rounds", each assessed by expert panels using structured scoring sheets, with certification requiring at least a “good” rating in all three modules. It functions as a faculty development intervention intended to standardize preceptor qualifications.
requirements: Candidates must meet eligibility criteria including a full-time bachelor's degree or higher, over 5 years of specialty experience (≥3 for postgraduates), an intermediate professional title or higher, and some internship teaching experience.
constraints: The article states the system was developed and implemented within a single tertiary hospital under a college–hospital collaborative model and "may limit cross-institutional standardization".
target_learners: Clinical nursing chief teachers (lead clinical instructors) at teaching hospitals
target_learning_goals: Standardized clinical teaching competency, including theory teaching, skill demonstration, and interactive teaching ward rounds
examples: Each department recommended 1–2 candidates assessed in 2021 onward; 152 of 193 candidates were certified, and certified preceptors were assigned to departments to undertake teaching responsibilities.

citation: Cheung H. C. Kristy, Zhong Lily Shengjia, Wall Shelley L., Lisk Kristina. (2026). Exploring the impact of virtual reality anatomy training on preparing biomedical illustrators for drawing anatomical structures. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70150
title: Linton's perception-versus-cognition account of 3D vision, used to explain prosection's advantage over 2D for depth depiction
description: The article invokes Linton's theory that understanding 3D space involves "two distinct processes: the perception and cognition of depth." Stereo depth cues are described as innate and requiring little cognitive effort, whereas pictorial depth cues require higher-level cognitive processing and constitute the cognition of depth, an acquired skill. The authors use this distinction to explain why participants depicted spatial relationships more effectively with prosections (stereo cues) than with 2D images (pictorial cues only).
requirements: Learners must be able to access stereo depth cues for perception of depth to occur without heavy cognitive processing
constraints: The article applies the theory interpretively; it did not directly test the mechanism, and notes vergence-accommodation conflict may hinder cognitive processing of VR-generated stereo cues
target_learners: graduate biomedical illustration students learning anatomy
target_learning_goals: perceiving and depicting depth and spatial relationships of anatomical structures
examples: The authors used the distinction to interpret why 2D-referenced drawings scored highest overall while prosection-referenced drawings were superior on depth-related rubric components

title: LISA-AT: a simulation-based assessment tool for less invasive surfactant administration competence
description: The LISA-AT is a rating instrument developed by international Delphi consensus (153 experts from 14 countries) to support operator training and competence assessment for LISA. It originally contained 15 metrics rated on a Likert scale of one to five with descriptive anchors for scores one, three, and five, plus a global pass/borderline/fail rating scale. In this study seven non-discriminating metrics were removed, leaving a modified 8-metric score ranging from 8–40 points, used for both formative feedback after each attempt and summative determination of the minimum passing score.

examples: Used onsite by trained investigators to score 33 participants' simulated LISA performances and to time feedback after each novice attempt

title: Live dynamic student-to-teacher gaze displays for one-to-one teaching
description: Gaze displays are "visualizations of where a student looks while executing a task", produced by eye-tracking apparatus (SMI RED250mobile, 250 Hz) and shown to the teacher in real time on a separate monitor during one-to-one teaching. The novel application is helping teachers spot covert misconceptions — for example, a student looking at the outermost retinal layer while speaking about the innermost — and adapt support accordingly. article_title: Small programs, big challenges: Reimagining the evaluation of clinical teaching in genetic counseling.
citation: Randall Armel, S. (2025). Small programs, big challenges: Reimagining the evaluation of clinical teaching in genetic counseling. Journal of Genetic Counseling, 34, e1924. https://doi.org/10.1002/jgc4.1924
title: Limit SETs to aspects students are equipped to assess and triangulate with other data sources
description: The review recommends restricting SETs to factors students have the knowledge and capacity to judge — workload, sense of the learning environment, the student–teacher relationship, teacher availability, clarity of goals and expectations, and timeliness and clarity of feedback — while leaving instructor knowledge, assessment quality, and instructional methods to other sources. It argues "triangulating SETs with other data points is critical" because SETs alone do not measure teaching effectiveness and are subject to gender and racial bias. Where other sources are unavailable, reflective practice should supplement SETs.
requirements: Accreditation standards should clarify the intended purpose of collecting SETs so programs do not implement measures that fail to ensure an inclusive learning environment
constraints: Most genetic counselors are evaluated for teaching by an institution that does not employ them, making multi-source evaluation challenging; most clinical teaching occurs pre or post patient encounter, limiting patient feedback
target_learners: clinical teachers and supervisors in health professions programs
target_learning_goals: accurate evaluation of clinical teaching effectiveness
improvement of teaching practice
examples: The review recommends genetic counseling programs implement processes using self-reflection, teaching self-assessments, and possibly self-efficacy scales to guide reflective practice and identify areas for skill development

citation: van Rijt, Jimmy; Myhill, Debra; De Maeyer, Sven; Coppen, Peter-Arno. (2022). Linguistic metaconcepts can improve grammatical understanding in L1 education: evidence from a Dutch quasi-experimental study. PLoS ONE 17(2): e0263123. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0263123
title: Linguistic metaconcepts as higher-order concepts that organize lower-order grammatical concepts
description: The article defines linguistic metaconcepts as concepts from modern linguistic theory that conceptually overarch traditional school grammar concepts. Linguistic metaconcepts "can thus be defined as 'higher-order concepts that facilitate the understanding or categorization of the lower-order concepts they thematically organize'". For example, the metaconcept of valency (the grammatical and semantic selection of arguments by verbs) underlies and helps students understand traditional concepts such as direct and indirect objects, which are often misunderstood without it. The relationship is one-directional: metaconcepts are used to understand lower-order concepts, not the reverse.
requirements: Traditional grammatical concepts must already be familiar to some degree so the metaconcept can refine and organize them
constraints: Research into metaconceptual approaches in L1 grammar learning has been quite scarce, per the article
target_learners: secondary school students in L1 (Dutch) education
target_learning_goals: grammatical understanding of the language system
examples: The intervention taught valency first, then used it to make sense of subjects, direct objects and indirect objects

citation: Schiffman J, Laski EV. (2018). Linear-spatial materials improve young children's addition strategies and accuracy, irregular arrays don't. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0208832
title: Represent quantities linearly rather than as random collections when instructing early arithmetic
description: The article concludes that "representing quantities linearly, rather than as random collections of objects or drawings, would be most efficacious for arithmetic instruction in early elementary school." Materials should instantiate the linear-spatial features of the mental number line — discrete units organized left to right with length correlated with number — so that practice activates children's existing magnitude representations and supports advanced strategies like count-on. The principle follows from the randomized experiment showing greater accuracy and strategy gains with linear-spatial than irregular materials.
requirements: Learners must possess some existing linear representation of numerical magnitude for the materials to activate.
constraints: Evidence comes from a small sample (n = 29) of low-income kindergartners with short-term outcomes; the article calls for testing with larger, more diverse groups and examining persistence of benefits.
target_learning_goals: addition accuracy on unpracticed problems
spontaneous use of advanced addition strategies
examples: Children played the Building Tens game with squares organized linearly on wooden sticks segmented into 2-cm units, versus stars in random arrays on cards; both conditions received identical game procedures and count-on practice.

citation: Klerman Elizabeth B., Beckett Scott A., Landrigan Christopher P. (2016). Applying mathematical models to predict resident physician performance and alertness on traditional and novel work schedules. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0751-9
title: Two linked mathematical models of circadian phase and wake duration predicting objective performance and subjective alertness
description: The article applies two linked mathematical models: "a model of the effect of light on the circadian pacemaker and a model of the effects of circadian phase and length of time awake on human objective performance (as measured by 'Cognitive Throughput') and on subjective alertness." The pacemaker model estimates circadian phase and amplitude from light exposure timing and intensity; the performance and alertness models then predict minute-level outputs. The models capture a non-linear interaction in which performance and alertness worsen with extended wake and at circadian night but can partially rebound during circadian day.
requirements: Light exposure timing and intensity as input to the circadian pacemaker model, and scheduled sleep episodes, to predict circadian phase, performance and alertness
constraints: The article notes the models in practice "do not take into account all of the features of the operational environment" and lack a chronic sleep restriction term in the current software
target_learners: Resident physicians (interns and senior residents) working shift-based hospital schedules
target_learning_goals: Predicting and minimizing performance and alertness decrements across work schedules
examples: The models were validated with experimental and field-based data and reported to yield good predictions for the range of sleep-wake schedules and light levels encountered by training physicians
